slides.section: 1. Three questions before prescribing anything
paragraphs: Does the patient have symptomatic infection? Is there an anatomic or functional reason for recurrence? Which preventive approach has a reasonable chance of helping without causing greater harm?

Recurrent uncomplicated cystitis generally means at least two separate symptomatic, culture-supported episodes within six months, or at least three in 12 months, with resolution between episodes. Persistent symptoms without resolution are not simply another recurrence.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
1. Three questions before prescribing anything Does the patient have symptomatic infection? Is there an anatomic or functional reason for recurrence? Which preventive approach has a reasonable chance of helping without causing greater harm? Recurrent uncomplicated cystitis generally means at least two separate symptomatic, culture-supported episodes within six months, or at least three in 12 months, with resolution between episodes. Persistent symptoms without resolution are not simply another recurrence. The 2025 AUA guidance primarily addresses otherwise healthy women with recurrent localized cystitis. The IDSA 2025 complicated-UTI guideline addresses acute treatment, not prevention of recurrent cystitis. Patients with devices, neurogenic bladder, stones, obstruction or recurrent febrile infections warrant individualized evaluation; prophylaxis trials in otherwise healthy women may not apply. IDSA 2025 classifies uncomplicated UTI as infection apparently confined to the bladder, in either sex. Fever, rigors, flank pain, CVA tenderness, bacteremia or other extension beyond the bladder suggest cUTI. Symptomatic infections with long-term catheters, stents or nephrostomy tubes are also included as cUTI. Male sex, diabetes, immunocompromise, BPH or cystocele alone do not automatically make an infection complicated. Evaluate risk factors separately and exclude prostatitis when relevant in men. Trautner et al., IDSA cUTI guideline 2025, classification .

slides.title: 2. Symptoms matter more than a positive culture
slides.section: 2. Symptoms matter more than a positive culture
rows: New dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic discomfort, sometimes visible hematuria

Compatible with acute cystitis, especially when new relative to baseline. Obtain urinalysis and urine culture for each suspected recurrence before antibiotics when feasible. Interpret contamination and prior culture history.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
2. Symptoms matter more than a positive culture Presentation Interpretation and action New dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic discomfort, sometimes visible hematuria Compatible with acute cystitis, especially when new relative to baseline. Obtain urinalysis and urine culture for each suspected recurrence before antibiotics when feasible. Interpret contamination and prior culture history. Fever, rigors, flank pain, CVA tenderness, vomiting, systemic illness Evaluate for pyelonephritis, obstruction, bacteremia, and other sources. Assess severity, renal function, and need for imaging or admission. Positive culture but no attributable urinary symptoms Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB), usually do not treat regardless of pyuria, odor, cloudiness, organism, or colony count. Main exceptions are pregnancy and before endoscopic urologic procedures with anticipated mucosal trauma. Chronic urgency, nocturia, incontinence, pelvic pain without a convincing new change Do not equate chronic baseline symptoms or pyuria with active UTI. Evaluate noninfectious causes. Delirium or fall alone in an older adult with bacteriuria, no focal urinary or systemic signs Search for other causes and observe. Positive culture alone does not establish infection. In hemodynamic instability, evaluate and treat suspected sepsis without assuming a urinary source. Catheter or spinal cord injury Chronic bacteriuria is expected. New fever, malaise, autonomic dysreflexia, spasticity, pelvic/flank discomfort, catheter obstruction, or other new compatible findings may prompt evaluation. Symptoms can be atypical; do not screen or treat stable bacteriuria. Pyuria supports inflammation but is not proof of UTI. Absence of pyuria in a patient with typical baseline immune function should prompt reconsideration. A positive culture without a compatible syndrome may be colonization; a negative culture during symptoms warrants reassessment, particularly if collected before antibiotics. AUA 2025; IDSA ASB guideline 2019. See references.

Symptoms matter more than a positive culture Presentation Interpretation and action New dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic discomfort, sometimes visible hematuria Compatible with acute cystitis, especially when new relative to baseline. Obtain urinalysis and urine culture for each suspected recurrence before antibiotics when feasible. Interpret contamination and prior culture history. Fever, rigors, flank pain, CVA tenderness, vomiting, systemic illness Evaluate for pyelonephritis, obstruction, bacteremia, and other sources. slides.title: 4. Look for a persistent reservoir when the pattern warrants it
slides.section: 4. Look for a persistent reservoir when the pattern warrants it
paragraphs: Compare dates, species, susceptibilities, symptom-free intervals, and antibiotic exposure. Prompt recurrence with the same organism shortly after apparently appropriate therapy raises concern for relapse, inadequate drug exposure, retained stone, obstruction, prostatic infection, or device biofilm. Repeated different isolates separated by wellness usually represent reinfection.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
4. Look for a persistent reservoir when the pattern warrants it Compare dates, species, susceptibilities, symptom-free intervals, and antibiotic exposure. Prompt recurrence with the same organism shortly after apparently appropriate therapy raises concern for relapse, inadequate drug exposure, retained stone, obstruction, prostatic infection, or device biofilm. Repeated different isolates separated by wellness usually represent reinfection. Clue Targeted workup Possible intervention Proteus, other urease-producing organisms, recurrent same isolate, stone history, hematuria Renal/bladder ultrasound or noncontrast CT when stone suspicion is high; assess stone burden and obstruction Urology for infected stone or staghorn calculus management. Antibiotics alone rarely sterilize a retained infected stone. High residual, weak stream, prolapse, neurogenic bladder, constipation, anticholinergic use Postvoid residual by bladder scan, medication review, pelvic/prostate examination; selective urodynamics Relieve retention, address prolapse/constipation, revise medications and catheterization plan. Hydronephrosis, recurrent pyelonephritis, renal dysfunction, flank pain Renal/bladder ultrasound, CT according to question and acuity; evaluate for obstruction Urgent decompression if infected obstructed system; later definitive source control. Catheter, stent, nephrostomy, foreign body Assess indication, drainage, exchange interval and obstruction; imaging if persistent symptoms Remove device when possible, replace when indicated. Do not attempt chronic urine sterilization. Pneumaturia/fecaluria, recurrent polymicrobial enteric flora CT abdomen/pelvis with appropriate protocol; urology/colorectal evaluation for fistula Manage fistula and associated bowel pathology. Unexplained gross hematuria or persistent microscopic hematuria after infection resolves Risk-based hematuria workup including cystoscopy and upper tract imaging when indicated Rule out malignancy rather than attributing all bleeding to UTI. slides.section: 5. Prevention options and what the trials actually show
rows: Vaginal estrogen, e.g., estradiol 10 micrograms vaginally twice weekly after a daily two-week initiation, or low-dose cream/ring
Recommended for peri/postmenopausal women with recurrent UTI when appropriate; improves local estrogen deficiency and reduces recurrence. Systemic estrogen is not a UTI preventive substitute.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
5. Prevention options and what the trials actually show Option Evidence / expected benefit Tolerability, limitations and cautions Vaginal estrogen, e.g., estradiol 10 micrograms vaginally twice weekly after a daily two-week initiation, or low-dose cream/ring Recommended for peri/postmenopausal women with recurrent UTI when appropriate; improves local estrogen deficiency and reduces recurrence. Systemic estrogen is not a UTI preventive substitute. Local irritation/discharge or spotting. Evaluate unexplained bleeding. Discuss breast cancer history with oncology when relevant; systemic absorption varies by preparation but is generally low with low-dose local therapy. Increase fluids if low intake In 140 premenopausal women drinking less than 1.5 L/day, an additional ~1.5 L water/day reduced mean cystitis episodes from 3.2 to 1.7 over 12 months. Trial applies to low baseline intake. Avoid forced fluids with heart failure, hyponatremia, or fluid restriction; may worsen frequency/nocturia. Cranberry products Modest preventive benefit in women with recurrent UTI; 2023 Cochrane estimate RR 0.74 (95% CI 0.55–0.99) for symptomatic culture-verified UTI in this subgroup. Juice sugar/calories, GI symptoms, inconsistent proanthocyanidin content; optimal product and dose not firmly established. Caution with warfarin interactions and stone history, especially concentrated high-oxalate products. Methenamine hippurate 1 g orally twice daily ALTAR: 1.38 versus 0.89 antibiotic-treated symptomatic episodes/person-year with methenamine versus daily antibiotic, difference 0.49 (90% CI 0.15–0.84); met prespecified noninferiority margin of 1 episode/person-year. GI upset, dysuria, rash. Needs acidic urine; avoid urinary alkalinizers and concurrent sulfonamides. Contraindicated with renal insufficiency, severe hepatic insufficiency, or severe dehydration by US label; no validated numerical CrCl threshold in US label. Not treatment for active UTI. Evidence best in women without urinary tract abnormalities. Do not routinely add vitamin C for acidification. Postcoital single-dose antibiotic Effective when episodes follow intercourse; often much less antibiotic exposure than daily suppression. Requires a clear trigger, susceptibility-informed selection; adverse effects and resistance remain possible. Patient-initiated short-course treatment Can shorten delay to treatment for patients who reliably recognize symptoms; not preventive. Collect urine before starting when practical and arrange follow-up if nonresponse, fever, or atypical symptoms. Avoid indiscriminate standing antibiotic use. Continuous low-dose antibiotic, usually trial 3–6 months then reassess Strong reduction in recurrences while taking therapy; recurrence often returns after discontinuation. slides.section: 6. Suppressive antibiotics when needed
paragraphs: These are example adult oral doses for prophylaxis of recurrent uncomplicated lower UTI, not acute infection, pyelonephritis, or chronic infected hardware/stone. Confirm recent susceptible isolates and local availability. Most use is off-label. Reassess efficacy, toxicities and indication after about three to six months rather than prescribing indefinitely by default.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
6. Suppressive antibiotics when needed These are example adult oral doses for prophylaxis of recurrent uncomplicated lower UTI, not acute infection, pyelonephritis, or chronic infected hardware/stone. Confirm recent susceptible isolates and local availability. Most use is off-label. Reassess efficacy, toxicities and indication after about three to six months rather than prescribing indefinitely by default. Drug Continuous dose Postcoital dose Major limitation Nitrofurantoin macrocrystals 50–100 mg PO nightly 50–100 mg PO once after intercourse For bladder only. Avoid with significant renal impairment; many contemporary practices use CrCl <30 mL/min as a cutoff for short courses, but long-term suppression at reduced CrCl is poorly studied and some US product labeling still states <60. Rare pulmonary fibrosis/pneumonitis, hepatitis, neuropathy, hemolysis with G6PD deficiency. Monitor symptoms and periodic renal/liver function. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 40/200 mg PO nightly or three times weekly 40/200 to 80/400 mg PO once Rash/SCAR, cytopenias, hyperkalemia, AKI, drug interactions (ACEi/ARB, spironolactone, warfarin); renal adjustment when CrCl <30. Monitor CBC, creatinine, potassium. Trimethoprim alone 100 mg PO nightly 100 mg PO once Hyperkalemia, marrow effects and renal adjustment; US availability varies. Cephalexin 125–250 mg PO nightly 250 mg PO once GI effects, candidiasis, C. difficile, selection of resistant flora; renal dose adjustment in CKD. Fosfomycin 3 g every 10 days appears in some European prophylaxis guidance but evidence and dosing intervals are less established in US practice; reserve for selected resistant-organism cases with ID/pharmacy input. Fluoroquinolones should generally not be used for chronic uncomplicated-cystitis suppression because of serious adverse effects and resistance selection. Do not use nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin when pyelonephritis or prostatitis is suspected. Renal function matters, but numerical cutoffs differ by drug and regulatory label. Methenamine has no universally validated US-label CrCl cutoff. A history of stones is a reason to evaluate composition and persistent infection, not an automatic contraindication to every prophylactic agent. Before starting suppression Document true symptomatic episode count, culture results, baseline renal function, medication interactions, pregnancy status where relevant, and prior adverse effects. Agree on the target (e.g., fewer symptomatic culture-confirmed episodes), duration, breakthrough-culture plan, and stopping point. Do not perform surveillance cultures while asymptomatic.

slides.title: 9. Acute complicated UTI and the 2025 IDSA guideline
slides.section: 9. Acute complicated UTI and the 2025 IDSA guideline
paragraphs: These recommendations apply to acute cUTI, including pyelonephritis, not asymptomatic bacteriuria or routine recurrent-cystitis prevention.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
9. Acute complicated UTI and the 2025 IDSA guideline These recommendations apply to acute cUTI, including pyelonephritis, not asymptomatic bacteriuria or routine recurrent-cystitis prevention. Decision Recommended approach and limitation Empiric therapy Assess severity and sepsis first, then recent urine cultures and resistance, prior antibiotic exposure, patient-specific adverse effects, and the local antibiogram when septic. Avoid agents with recent documented resistance. The guideline suggests avoiding fluoroquinolones if exposed to that class in the prior 12 months. Nonseptic cUTI does not automatically warrant a carbapenem or a novel agent. Culture results De-escalate to the narrowest effective regimen once susceptibilities are available. An effective cUTI antibiotic must reach the urine and relevant tissue; bloodstream exposure also matters with bacteremia. IV to oral Switch if clinically improving, able to take oral medication, and an active oral agent is available. In selected Gram-negative bacteremia, this is reasonable after stability and source control. Trials underrepresented severe sepsis, catheterized patients, immunocompromise, severe renal insufficiency and structural abnormalities. Duration For improving cUTI, use 5–7 days of an effective fluoroquinolone or 7 days of an effective non-fluoroquinolone, counted from the first day of effective therapy. In improving cUTI with Gram-negative bacteremia, 7 days is suggested over 14 days. Exceptions and uncertainty Individualize with inadequate source control, urinary abscess, complete obstruction, severe sepsis, indwelling devices, CKD or substantial immunocompromise; many trials excluded these patients. Suspected acute bacterial prostatitis in febrile men may warrant 10–14 days. Evidence for short-course oral beta-lactams in cUTI is more limited and adequate dosing is important. Failure to improve promptly should trigger reassessment for obstruction, retained stone, abscess, inadequate drug exposure or another diagnosis rather than automatic antibiotic extension. The cUTI guideline does not provide a treatment algorithm for chronic urinary symptoms. Trautner et al., IDSA 2025 cUTI guideline: empiric and definitive therapy, IV-to-oral transition, and duration .

slides.section: 8. Cases for discussion
paragraphs: Do not treat ASB. Determine what, if anything, changed from baseline. Evaluate atrophy, incontinence, retention, medications, and bladder symptoms. A resistant isolate does not convert colonization into infection.

8. Cases for discussion A 71-year-old with chronic frequency, no new urinary symptoms, and urine culture with ESBL E. coli . She has requested another antibiotic. Discussion Do not treat ASB. Determine what, if anything, changed from baseline. Evaluate atrophy, incontinence, retention, medications, and bladder symptoms. A resistant isolate does not convert colonization into infection. A 39-year-old has four culture-confirmed cystitis episodes in a year, each within 48 hours after intercourse. Normal exam, no hematuria, no febrile episodes. Discussion No routine CT or cystoscopy. Avoid spermicide, discuss postcoital prophylaxis based on susceptibility versus patient-initiated treatment, and review whether nonantibiotic measures are preferred. A 63-year-old has recurrent Proteus bacteriuria and febrile episodes after antibiotics. She has a history of stones. slides.section: Relapse, devices and special populations
paragraphs: Repeated same-species growth does not prove a genetically identical strain. A short symptom-free interval after apparently adequate therapy changes the probability of a reservoir and should prompt review of culture collection, adherence, drug penetration, upper tract involvement, and device/stone status. Consider prostatic infection in men and occult obstruction with febrile relapses.

Consider prostatic infection in men and occult obstruction with febrile relapses. In indwelling-catheter or intermittent-catheter users, avoid routine prophylaxis and surveillance cultures as a default. Assess obstruction, catheter necessity and technique, bladder pressures/emptying, and stone burden. Evidence from uncomplicated women is not directly applicable. In neurogenic bladder, distinguish individual baseline symptoms and true new changes; specialist evaluation may be necessary. Pregnancy has different screening, treatment and prophylaxis decisions.

slides.title: Stones, urinary pH and preventive products
slides.section: Stones, urinary pH and preventive products
paragraphs: Struvite stones arise with urease-producing organisms; remove infected stone burden when feasible. Other stones can still predispose to recurrent infection through obstruction or bacterial persistence. Consider stone analysis and metabolic evaluation for recurrent stone formers. High-dose ascorbic acid may increase urinary oxalate. Cranberry products are not proven to prevent stones and concentrated products may add oxalate; the magnitude of stone risk varies by formulation and evidence is limited.
slides.notes:

Stones, urinary pH and preventive products Struvite stones arise with urease-producing organisms; remove infected stone burden when feasible. Other stones can still predispose to recurrent infection through obstruction or bacterial persistence. Consider stone analysis and metabolic evaluation for recurrent stone formers. High-dose ascorbic acid may increase urinary oxalate. Cranberry products are not proven to prevent stones and concentrated products may add oxalate; the magnitude of stone risk varies by formulation and evidence is limited. Methenamine hydrolyzes to formaldehyde in acidic urine, with poor activity when urine is alkaline. Proteus may alkalinize urine, undermining efficacy. Methenamine is not a replacement for drainage of infected obstruction. US labeling contraindicates renal insufficiency without specifying a CrCl threshold; do not present a fixed cutoff as a product-label fact. Some trials excluded advanced CKD, so extrapolation is unsafe.

slides.title: Evidence limits and shared decisions
slides.section: Evidence limits and shared decisions
paragraphs: ALTAR was open-label and used episodes requiring antibiotics as its principal outcome; its noninferiority margin allowed as many as one additional UTI per person-year with methenamine. Patients need the absolute event rates, not just the word “noninferior.” Long-term antibiotic prevention works during exposure but may select resistant flora. Trials frequently exclude significant urinary tract abnormalities and advanced CKD.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:

Patients need the absolute event rates, not just the word “noninferior.” Long-term antibiotic prevention works during exposure but may select resistant flora. Trials frequently exclude significant urinary tract abnormalities and advanced CKD. For the patient with frequent symptom reports and intermittent normal cultures, offer symptom-triggered urine testing with a documented threshold for treatment. A standing culture order can be reasonable; automatic antibiotics after a positive result are not. Agree to revisit the diagnosis if symptoms and microbiology repeatedly diverge.
